Risks.riskTitle: Data Hub field dependency may delay total premium implementation
Risks.riskDescription: The project is awaiting 4 additional fields needed for total premium calculation from DH on 30th July, and if those fields are received on that date the changes can only be made by 5th August, creating a schedule risk for the current implementation work.

riskChain.rootCause: Upstream Data Hub dependency for 4 total premium fields needed to complete BoB premium calculation.
riskChain.trigger: DH provides the fields late, incomplete, or with values requiring additional validation or transformation.
riskChain.primaryRisk: Total premium implementation for Book of Business is delayed during Implement & Build.
riskChain.downstreamRisk: Integration testing, E2E validation, and UAT scenarios for premium-related BoB functionality are compressed or deferred.
riskChain.impact: Schedule slippage can affect BoB readiness, reduce test window, and pressure the 2-Sep rollout path.

Risks.businessImpact: Book of Business is a core in-scope portal capability. Delay in total premium logic can reduce functional completeness, affect producer-facing financial display, and compress dependent integration, E2E, and UAT activities.
Risks.currentProjectEvidence: WSR Open Items dated 7/3/2026 states 4 additional fields are needed for total premium calculation and if made available on 30th July, changes can only be made by 5th August. Project Health Summary also states schedule depends on DH availability of 4 total premium fields. Dependencies & Blockers item 26 remains open for confirmation on total premium fields shared by business.
Risks.currentContextReasoning: The project is in Implement & Build with PI6 UAT & Roll-out ahead and rollout targeted for 2nd Sept. Because BoB and dashboard integration are central scope items, a late Data Hub field dependency now affects not just build completion but downstream test readiness and acceptance sequencing.

historicalCorrelation.similarHistoricalPattern: Premera Blue Cross - AI Platform Build - Claims historical risk showed upstream FACETS integration decision latency limiting task readiness and causing utilization and schedule pressure.
historicalCorrelation.historicalReasoning: Historical dependency intelligence for project 119971 documented the chain: pending integration decision -> insufficient sprint-ready tasks -> reduced utilization -> delayed sprint commitments. This directly supports the current pattern of upstream dependency latency leading to schedule pressure.

Risks.futureRiskProjection: If the fields are not consumable by the expected date, premium logic will likely spill further into August, causing partial E2E coverage and potential UAT execution with known functional gaps or rushed retesting.
Risks.recurrenceJustification: Historical Premera evidence shows dependency-latency repeatedly affecting work readiness and delivery timelines. The current project exhibits the same dependency-driven delivery pattern, with stronger direct schedule evidence.
Risks.leadingIndicators: DH ETA moves beyond 30th July; unclear field definitions persist; mapping/value clarifications increase; premium stories remain open into August; E2E team defers premium scenarios.
Risks.predictiveInsight: This risk is likely to evolve from a build dependency into a testing-window compression risk unless Data Hub readiness is resolved with usable fields and confirmed values.
Risks.mitigation: Establish a date-bound Data Hub decision and delivery checkpoint with DH, business, and E2E stakeholders; complete implementation design and code scaffolding before field arrival; predefine test cases and mock-value validations so only final wiring remains after field release; isolate premium changes behind targeted regression scope to minimize retest spread.
Risks.recommendations: 1. Run daily dependency triage with DH until field delivery is confirmed and value semantics are signed off. 2. Freeze premium calculation assumptions and document fallback behavior for missing fields. 3. Prepare a separate premium regression pack for rapid execution after implementation. 4. Escalate by governance if field readiness slips beyond recovery threshold for PI5/PI6.

riskChain.trigger: Premera does not complete the DB connection configuration update on time or propagation issues emerge during environment promotion.
riskChain.primaryRisk: Move to ACPT is delayed or blocked.
riskChain.downstreamRisk: Authentication-dependent integration, validation, and deployment-readiness activities slip.
riskChain.impact: Testing and release-preparation timelines compress, especially for identity-linked scenarios.

Risks.businessImpact: Authentication and authorization are explicit in-scope capabilities. Delay in ACPT identity configuration affects environment readiness, deployment validation, and execution of Auth0/Entra dependent flows before UAT.
Risks.currentProjectEvidence: WSR Open Items dated 7/6/2026 states DB connection configuration is maintained outside Auth0 and needs Premera team update because project team lacks ACPT tenant access. Project Health Summary also lists Auth0 integration with Entra as a schedule dependency.
Risks.currentContextReasoning: The project relies on Auth0 and Azure AD/Entra integration, and ACPT deployment is part of current sprint readiness. Since identity readiness gates other functional validation, this risk can block more than configuration work alone.

historicalCorrelation.similarHistoricalPattern: Premera Claims historical evidence showed external stakeholder decisions and access dependencies constraining sprint readiness and delivery flow.
historicalCorrelation.historicalReasoning: Historical patterns support the broader cause-effect chain of external dependency -> blocked work progression -> delivery delay, though the current risk is identity-configuration specific.

Risks.recommendations: 1. Confirm a committed Premera owner and execution slot for ACPT config update. 2. Schedule joint validation immediately after change completion. 3. riskChain.impact: Late-cycle rework delays schedule and weakens acceptance readiness.

Risks.currentProjectEvidence: Open item dated 6/25/2026 states if issues with mapped values lead back to design/entity stitching, there may be time impact. Scope Change Tracker items 13, 15, 24, and 31 show multiple changes involving BoB DH API orchestration, additional entities to stitch, company mapping availability, and ongoing discussion of possible values. Key Decision Item 19 documents proceeding with UI-based schema to mitigate timeline risk while accepting possible rework.
Risks.currentContextReasoning: The project has already absorbed contract-schema development, synthetic data use, and later Data Hub integration. That means mapping defects are likely to emerge during integrated validation rather than earlier local development, which makes downstream impact more severe.

historicalCorrelation.similarHistoricalPattern: Premera Servicing historical evidence showed dependency mapping changes mid-sprint contributing to code quality friction and delivery concern.
historicalCorrelation.historicalReasoning: Historical cluster 119972-C1 documented mapping changes and weak review controls causing quality and delivery friction. This supports the pattern that unstable mapping assumptions can surface later as quality or schedule issues.

Risks.futureRiskProjection: If mapping confidence remains incomplete, the next likely developments are failed integrated scenarios, business clarification loops, wrapper-service redesign, and repeated regression effort.

Risks.leadingIndicators: Repeated mapping clarification calls; frequent updates to stitching logic; BoB or export inconsistencies; failing E2E scenarios tied to data values; rising defects in integrated data paths.
Risks.predictiveInsight: The highest risk is late discovery of semantic mapping errors after progress appears healthy, which can rapidly convert into schedule-consuming rework.
Risks.mitigation: Institute field-level semantic signoff for critical BoB data elements; create a controlled mapping baseline and change log; run handshake validation with DH and business on stitched outputs before broader E2E execution.
Risks.recommendations: 1. Prioritize high-impact fields such as premium, company, producer/agency stitching, and plan details for early validation. 2. Add targeted integration tests around mapped values, not just API connectivity. 3. Freeze mapping changes after signoff unless governance-approved. 4. Reserve rework capacity in sprint plan for data-correction scenarios.

historicalCorrelation.similarHistoricalPattern: Premera Claims historical evidence showed offshore delivery fragility caused by operating constraints and lack of inclusion, affecting utilization and quality.
historicalCorrelation.historicalReasoning: Historical support is directional rather than infrastructure-specific, but it does show offshore constraints can amplify delivery risk.

Risks.predictiveInsight: This risk is most dangerous as a multiplier: it reduces the team's ability to absorb late dependency changes or quality corrections.
Risks.mitigation: Log and quantify Citrix productivity loss by team and activity type; establish alternate access paths where possible; shift priority work requiring stable connectivity to unaffected windows or users until issue stabilizes.
Risks.recommendations: 1. Escalate Citrix performance as an operational blocker with measurable impact. 2. Capture time lost and affected work items for governance review. 3. Re-sequence work so high-latency tasks are minimized during peak issue periods. 4. Prepare contingency resource rotation for critical deployment and test windows.

historicalCorrelation.similarHistoricalPattern: Premera Claims historical evidence showed pending upstream decisions limiting task readiness and utilization.

Track non-deterministic behavior separately from standard defects. 4. Avoid expanding agent scope until hardening evidence is available.

historicalCorrelation.similarHistoricalPattern: Premera historical intelligence consistently shows dependency uncertainty causing readiness and quality pressure.

Open items include total premium fields and mapping/design uncertainty. Current Sprint Goals and readiness also show Data Hub dependencies for BoB and data setup.
Risks.currentContextReasoning: Multiple open issues converge on the same dependency family: fields, data values, entity stitching, NPN search support, and test data. This makes Data Hub readiness the dominant schedule driver rather than an isolated issue.

historicalCorrelation.similarHistoricalPattern: Premera Claims historical evidence documented upstream integration decision latency reducing work readiness and threatening timelines.
historicalCorrelation.historicalReasoning: Historical observation, pattern intelligence, dependency intelligence, and root cause intelligence all identify dependency latency as a frequent failure driver. The current project presents a stronger and more direct manifestation of that same pattern.

Risks.futureRiskProjection: If Data Hub readiness remains unstable, late-cycle integration defects, compressed E2E/UAT, possible deferral of lower-priority fixes, and elevated release risk are likely.
Risks.recurrenceJustification: Historical Premera evidence strongly supports dependency-latency recurrence, and current project evidence is extensive and multi-source.
Risks.leadingIndicators: DH dates move again; open dependency items remain unresolved into August; mock/synthetic testing persists; E2E data setup remains incomplete; integration defects cluster around BoB/Dashboard flows.
Risks.predictiveInsight: This is the central risk propagation chain in the project: unresolved Data Hub readiness can cascade into build completion, testing quality, acceptance timing, and release confidence.
Risks.mitigation: Manage Data Hub as a formal critical path workstream with daily cross-team governance, recovery thresholds, and decision escalations; maintain a prioritized fallback test and delivery plan for scenarios not blocked by DH readiness.
Risks.recommendations: 1. Establish an executive-visible dependency tracker for all Data Hub blockers. 2. Define red-line dates beyond which rollout or scope decisions must be made. 3. Separate must-have vs deferrable DH-dependent functionality. 4. Align E2E, UAT, and pen test schedules to realistic DH readiness rather than optimistic assumptions.

Risks.riskTitle: Limited scope visibility may reduce work allocation and affect delivery quality
Risks.riskDescription: The project runs in a T&M model with no onshore presence and an offshore team working directly with the McK team, while the team lacked overall context and design visibility and was not consistently included in key Scrum meetings, leading to no work allocation for a few engineers and creating billing and quality concerns.

riskChain.rootCause: Offshore-only execution in a T&M model with limited inclusion in program management, design, and key Scrum ceremonies.
riskChain.trigger: Requirement/task changes continue while the team remains inconsistently included in context-setting discussions.
riskChain.primaryRisk: Task clarity and work allocation remain incomplete.
riskChain.downstreamRisk: Idle capacity, billing exposure, and quality concerns increase.
riskChain.impact: Financial, delivery, and client relationship risk materialize.

Risks.businessImpact: Because the project objective involved claims SOP automation and FACETS-linked work, incomplete scope/design visibility reduced the team's ability to convert demand into productive delivery, directly affecting utilization and delivery quality.
Risks.currentProjectEvidence: Risk register states no onshore and only offshore team working directly with McK who owns program management, sprint, and design. Team lacked overall context and design, had changing requirements and skill/task allocations, and was not consistently included in all key Scrum meetings. Consequence recorded included no work allocation for some engineers, billing impact, and quality concerns.
Risks.currentContextReasoning: This was a governance and execution weakness embedded in the operating model. The root cause directly explains why utilization and quality exposure emerged despite available engineers.

historicalCorrelation.similarHistoricalPattern: Historical cluster 119971-C1: Scope Visibility and Delivery Governance Gap.
historicalCorrelation.historicalReasoning: Historical evidence for the same project documented the exact pattern: limited offshore visibility into scope/design + inconsistent Scrum inclusion -> inadequate task clarity -> idle capacity and quality risk. Mitigations of daily connects and single POC improved tactical control.

Risks.futureRiskProjection: If this project had remained active without structural correction, the most likely next stage would have been recurring underutilization, more context-driven rework, and increased scrutiny on billing and delivery quality.
Risks.recurrenceJustification: Exact same project historical evidence confirms this risk chain and its downstream effects.
Risks.leadingIndicators: Missed ceremony invitations; engineers without sprint-ready work; heavy reliance on recordings for design context; frequent task reallocations; quality questions linked to missing business context.
Risks.predictiveInsight: In offshore-heavy T&M engagements, exclusion from high-context decisions rapidly converts into both financial and quality risk.
Risks.mitigation: Daily connects with a single POC, access to design call recordings, and direct client-lead alignment were historically effective tactical controls for restoring visibility and work continuity.
Risks.recommendations: 1. Make design and key Scrum participation mandatory for offshore leads from project start. 2. Establish a single operational POC plus decision log for scope/task clarity. 3. Convert ad hoc recordings into structured design handoff summaries. 4. In similar future projects, review ceremony inclusion as an early delivery-control checkpoint.

Risks.riskTitle: Pending FACETS integration decision may limit task readiness and utilization
Risks.riskDescription: Sprint commitments and resource allocation depended on finalizing the FACETS integration approach and related leadership decisions, and because the final approach was pending the project had limited PBI and task readiness for offshore engineers, creating reduced utilization and delayed sprint progress risk.

riskChain.rootCause: Pending leadership decision on FACETS integration approach after workshop discussions on data retrieval options.
riskChain.trigger: Final integration direction is not confirmed in time for sprint planning and backlog preparation.
riskChain.primaryRisk: PBIs and tasks are not sprint-ready.
riskChain.downstreamRisk: Offshore utilization declines and sprint commitments slip.
riskChain.impact: Revenue, utilization, and timeline pressure increase.

Risks.businessImpact: FACETS integration was central to claims SOP automation. Delayed integration direction blocked translation of project scope into executable backlog, reducing productive capacity and threatening delivery commitments.
Risks.currentProjectEvidence: Risk register states workshop discussed multiple FACETS integration approaches but final leadership decision was pending, impacting PBI/task readiness and limiting task availability for offshore engineers. Consequence recorded was reduced utilization and delayed sprint progress.
Risks.currentContextReasoning: This was a classic work-readiness dependency. The issue was not lack of resources but lack of released and decision-backed work for those resources.

historicalCorrelation.similarHistoricalPattern: Historical cluster 119971-C2: Work Readiness Dependency and Utilization Risk.
historicalCorrelation.historicalReasoning: The same project's historical evidence documented the exact chain: pending FACETS decision -> insufficient sprint-ready PBIs/tasks -> reduced utilization -> delayed sprint commitments. Mitigation to expedite decisions and prepare alternate work was only partially structural.

Risks.futureRiskProjection: Had the project continued without timely integration direction, the likely next pattern would have been more idle capacity followed by compressed execution once direction was finalized, increasing schedule and quality stress.
Risks.recurrenceJustification: This exact risk pattern is historically confirmed in the same project and supported by portfolio-level trend intelligence on dependency latency.
Risks.leadingIndicators: Backlog lacks sprint-ready PBIs; spikes replace committed work; external decision dates move; engineers diverted to alternate work; sprint commitments hinge on unresolved upstream decisions.
Risks.predictiveInsight: Architecture decision latency often shows up first as a utilization problem before it becomes an obvious schedule failure.
Risks.mitigation: Historically, requesting expedited decisions and preparing alternate sprint-ready work items reduced immediate idle time, though evidence shows this was only partially successful because the structural dependency remained.
Risks.recommendations: 1. In similar future projects, define decision SLAs for architecture/integration choices before sprint planning. 2. Maintain a pre-approved alternate backlog for dependency-heavy workstreams. 3. Separate spike work from commitment-bearing delivery to protect say/do accuracy. 4. Escalate unresolved integration decisions earlier through governance rather than absorbing delay operationally.

majorBottlenecks: Limited offshore visibility into scope and design decisions
Inconsistent inclusion in key Scrum meetings
FACETS integration approach pending on leadership decisions
riskPropagationPatterns: Scope/design visibility gap -> unclear task allocation -> idle capacity -> billing and quality exposure
Pending integration decision -> insufficient sprint-ready backlog -> reduced utilization -> delayed sprint commitments
emergingConcerns: Reactive coordination was stronger than proactive integration
Delivery issues accumulated and were tactically managed until project closure rather than structurally eliminated
highRiskDependencies: Inclusion in Scrum and design governance
rootCauseConcentration: Insufficient embedding of offshore teams in high-context delivery flow
mostLikelyFailureTriggers: Delayed leadership decisions on integration approach
Requirement shifts without corresponding context handoff
projectForecastInsights.overallOutlook: Historical project outlook was constrained by governance and work-readiness weaknesses rather than engineering capacity. The evidence shows tactical containment was possible, but structural operating-model issues were the main risk amplifier.

Risks.riskTitle: PR quality misalignment may affect team morale and stakeholder rapport
Risks.riskDescription: Concerns were received on code quality based on PR comments from McK, and the review found issues related to internal PR conversations and dependency mappings or changes mid sprint, which may create further misalignment and affect team morale and rapport with the full team.

riskChain.rootCause: PR feedback misalignment combined with mid-sprint dependency mapping changes and weak internal quality gate before external review.
riskChain.trigger: Code changes are exposed to external review before internal alignment and dependency impacts are stabilized.
riskChain.primaryRisk: Code review friction and perceived quality concerns recur.
riskChain.downstreamRisk: Team morale, rapport, and confidence in offshore rigor decline.

Risks.businessImpact: In an active AI delivery engagement, repeated review friction slows delivery, consumes lead effort, and can undermine trust in technical discipline even when some findings stem from process misalignment rather than defective code alone.
Risks.currentProjectEvidence: Risk register states concerns received on code quality based on PR comments from McK. Review found issues more related to internal PR conversations and dependency mappings/changes mid sprint. Consequence stated was impact to team morale and rapport if misalignment happened again.
Risks.currentContextReasoning: This was not only a code-quality issue; it was a quality-signaling issue occurring in collaborative review. Because dependency changes were occurring mid sprint, recurrence risk was credible without stronger internal controls.

historicalCorrelation.similarHistoricalPattern: Historical cluster 119972-C1: Code Review Quality Alignment Breakdown.
historicalCorrelation.historicalReasoning: The same project historically showed PR quality feedback misalignment, mid-sprint dependency changes, and weak internal review gates leading to reputational friction and morale impact. Stricter draft PR controls and training were successful mitigations.

Risks.futureRiskProjection: If internal quality alignment had not improved, this tactical issue would likely have escalated into broader stakeholder doubt about offshore technical rigor and delivery credibility.
Risks.recurrenceJustification: The project's historical lifecycle intelligence explicitly shows quality concern progression into wider confidence concerns.
Risks.leadingIndicators: Repeated PR comment themes; dependency changes continue mid sprint; longer PR turnaround; more lead time spent on pre-screening; declining team sentiment.
Risks.predictiveInsight: In this project, PR friction was an early-warning signal for strategic trust erosion, not just a local code review problem.
Risks.mitigation: Historically successful mitigation included stringent code review process, internal draft PR checks, gap identification, and training before external PR exposure.
Risks.recommendations: 1. Preserve mandatory internal draft PR and architecture review gates before McK-facing submissions. 2. Freeze dependency-related design changes before PR cut where possible. 3. Track repeated PR comment themes as a delivery health indicator. 4. Use lead-led quality coaching on areas repeatedly flagged in external review.

Risks.riskTitle: Gaps in visible AI expertise may erode client confidence
Risks.riskDescription: The client expects proactive AI-driven recommendations and value-added insights, but delivered code and outcomes have not consistently reflected the expected level of AI expertise and communication gaps have reduced confidence in offshore contributions, potentially leading to increased scrutiny, escalations, lower stakeholder satisfaction, reluctance to approve future work, and impact to project continuity.

riskChain.rootCause: Mismatch between client expectation of visible AI leadership and the team's demonstrated delivery, communication, and proactive solutioning.
riskChain.trigger: Delivery continues to appear reactive or insufficiently differentiated while communication gaps persist.
riskChain.primaryRisk: Client confidence in offshore AI capability declines further.
riskChain.downstreamRisk: Scrutiny, escalations, reluctance to approve future work, and account growth constraints intensify.
riskChain.impact: Project continuity, revenue opportunity, and reputation are affected.

Risks.businessImpact: This is an account-level risk, not just a sprint-performance issue. Because the client selected the organization for AI expertise and expects proactive value-add, failure to visibly demonstrate that capability can affect current delivery trust and future commercial opportunities.
Risks.currentProjectEvidence: Risk register states the client selected the organization based on proven AI expertise and expects proactive AI-driven recommendations and value-added insights. Delivered code and outcomes have not consistently reflected expected AI expertise, communication gaps reduced confidence, and lack of proactive solutioning created doubt about staffing capability. Consequences listed include scrutiny, escalations, lower satisfaction, reluctance to approve future work, and project/account continuity impact.
Risks.currentContextReasoning: This is strongly evidenced and strategically significant. The issue is not technical output alone but whether technical capability is visible, contextualized, and communicated in a way that matches client expectations for an AI engagement.

historicalCorrelation.similarHistoricalPattern: Historical cluster 119972-C2: Client Confidence Erosion in AI Delivery Capability.
historicalCorrelation.historicalReasoning: The same project's historical evidence documents this exact strategic pattern and lifecycle analysis shows tactical quality concerns expanded into wider capability perception and account-level risk. Historical mitigation remains unproven, indicating the risk is persistent and slower to resolve than technical defects.

Risks.futureRiskProjection: If confidence continues to erode, the most likely next developments are tighter governance oversight, executive escalation, slower approval of future work, and reduced willingness to continue or expand the engagement without visible corrective evidence.
Risks.recurrenceJustification: Exact historical evidence from the same project supports the same cause-event-consequence chain and shows strategic trust risks age longer than tactical delivery issues.
Risks.leadingIndicators: Requests for more demos and code walkthroughs; increased governance frequency; repeated questions about staffing fit; muted response to solution proposals; concerns raised beyond delivery leads to executive stakeholders.
Risks.predictiveInsight: This is the highest-consequence risk in Servicing because it can harden from delivery skepticism into commercial resistance if visible AI leadership does not improve quickly.
Risks.mitigation: Historically planned mitigation includes SME/circle-leader enablement, regular solution demonstrations, code walkthroughs, architectural contributions, improved stakeholder communication, AI-focused governance reporting, higher governance frequency, and executive engagement. Historical evidence marks this mitigation as still unproven because the risk remained assessed and active.
Risks.recommendations: 1. Convert AI capability into visible artifacts every sprint: solution notes, design options, demos, and measurable value-add callouts. 2. Pair offshore leads with SMEs for client-facing technical storytelling until confidence improves. 3. Include a formal capability-rebuild plan in governance with evidence-based progress markers. 4. Escalate from reactive reassurance to proactive architectural and innovation recommendations tied to project goals.

Mid-sprint dependency changes affecting quality signaling
Insufficient visible conversion of AI capability into client confidence
riskPropagationPatterns: PR quality friction -> stakeholder doubt on technical rigor -> reduced confidence in offshore contribution -> broader AI capability concern
Expectation gap on proactive AI solutioning -> increased scrutiny -> account-level trust erosion
emergingConcerns: Strategic trust risk persists longer than tactical quality issues
Technical competence alone is insufficient without visible solution leadership and communication quality
highRiskDependencies: Quality of proactive AI demonstrations and recommendations
rootCauseConcentration: Process and governance weakness in review flow
Capability signaling weakness relative to AI engagement expectations
mostLikelyFailureTriggers: Continued lack of proactive AI-driven recommendations
Client perception that offshore team capability does not match engagement promise
projectForecastInsights.overallOutlook: At risk from strategic trust erosion more than from unresolved coding defects alone. Historical evidence shows tactical quality issues can be contained, but confidence in AI delivery capability is slower to rebuild and materially affects continuity and growth.
